strengths: Well-motivated paradigm shift from centralized to distributed routing with clear articulation of limitations in existing approaches
Elegant scenario-conditioned reward function enabling adaptive behavior across cost-performance tradeoffs without retraining, with solid theoretical justification (Eq. 8-10, Figure 3)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning 10 datasets, 8 baselines, multiple scenarios, with consistent improvements across all configurations
Strong empirical evidence for core claim: intrinsic self-assessment (80% accuracy) substantially outperforms external classifiers (BERT 56%, LLM-8B 71%)
Thorough analysis of why the method works (Section 4.3): effective query difficulty discrimination, demonstrated self-awareness capability, and comparison with external routers
High reproducibility: open-source models/datasets, detailed implementation details, response templates, and comprehensive appendices enabling community validation
Good generalization: demonstrates strong performance on out-of-domain datasets and maintains modularity when agent pool size changes (3-agent system test)
weaknesses: Architectural validation limited to cascade structure only; claims about tree and mesh topologies lack empirical support and are deferred to future work despite being central to modularity claims
Incremental novelty: SFT approach builds directly on Xu et al. (2024), RL stage is standard Reinforce++; main contribution is combining existing techniques rather than fundamental innovation
Training cost analysis incomplete: requires 4×A100 for SFT + 8×A100 for RL per model, substantially higher than single-router training, yet practical deployment costs not quantified or discussed

Scenario adaptability robustness unclear: behavior when α changes at inference time unexplored; only three discrete scenarios tested; no prompt sensitivity analysis despite information provided via instructions

Experimental design concerns: GraphRouter requires scenario-specific retraining but is compared against single adaptive DiSRouter model (unfair comparison); Oracle only achieves 74-89% accuracy suggesting model selection may not be primary bottleneck

Data construction methodology lacks validation: assumes CoT sampling frequency correlates with true capability but this assumption is unvalidated; relies on external model (Qwen-14B) for answer extraction
Missing ablations: SFT vs SFT+RL contribution not isolated; reliability factor γ fixed at 0.5 without sensitivity analysis; cascade length effects not analyzed
Routing overhead dismissed as negligible (2-5%) but accumulates across cascade steps; total end-to-end latency impact and typical cascade depth not reported
Generalization limited in scope: OOD datasets (SQuAD, HellaSwag, HeadQA) remain similar to in-domain; no evaluation on different domains (code, translation, multimodal) or different LLM families
Modest improvements over strong baselines: +0.05 utility vs GraphRouter in Balance scenario (0.61 vs 0.53); no statistical significance testing to confirm improvements are meaningful
Practical deployment challenges unaddressed: how to maintain separate training for multiple models; impact of model updates/replacement; claimed scalability to hundreds of models not demonstrated
Analysis of failure modes absent: no discussion of when/why DiSRouter underperforms or specific query types with poor self-assessment

strengths: Clear motivation identifying genuine limitations of centralized routing (inflexibility, poor capability assessment)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation with multiple datasets (10 total), baselines (5+ methods), and scenarios (3 preference settings)
Solid analysis of why the method works (Section 4.3): self-assessment outperforms external routers, effective query difficulty discrimination
Thorough reproducibility support with detailed hyperparameters, prompts, and implementation details across appendices
Careful validation that training improvements are negligible (<1%, Appendix J), isolating gains to self-awareness rather than task performance
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: cascade architecture from FrugalGPT, rejection SFT from prior work (Xu et al. 2024), simple reward function. Main contribution is applying existing techniques in distributed setting—feels incremental

Overstated 'distributed' claims: only cascade evaluated despite claiming flexibility; agents restricted to routing toward higher-cost models; tree/mesh structures mentioned as future work, not contributions. System is a predetermined sequence, not truly distributed

Modest empirical improvements: Balance scenario 0.61 vs 0.53 for GraphRouter; out-of-domain 0.48 vs 0.39. Performance/Cost-First results relegated to appendices. Table 2 shows RL sometimes hurts performance

Evaluation fairness concerns: authors train LLMs (SFT+RL) while baselines don't; some baselines re-implemented with model substitutes; Table 5 compares 7B model against weaker external classifiers (strawman-like)

Methodological issues not explored: (1) SFT uses threshold δ=1-α but inference uses scenario prompts—interaction unclear; (2) γ=0.5 set without ablation or justification; (3) redundancy between scenario-aware training and prompt-based instructions unexplored
Missing critical ablations: no ablation on reward function components, sensitivity to γ, computational cost-benefit analysis of training vs. inference savings, error analysis of misrouted queries

Generalization limitations: single model family (Qwen 2.5), unclear with heterogeneous families; requires fine-tuning all models (impossible for proprietary APIs); QA-only evaluation, unclear for generation/reasoning tasks
Suspicious baseline results: Oracle 93% in-domain but 89% out-of-domain—larger gap than expected if routing to smallest capable model
Theoretical justification weak: Equations 5→6 decomposition assumes agent independence, but earlier agents' decisions affect which queries reach later agents
Scenario adaptability is straightforward: achieved via simple prompting + training variants. Not particularly novel

strengths: Novel and well-motivated distributed routing paradigm that addresses real limitations of centralized approaches (inflexibility and inaccurate capability assessment)
Comprehensive experimental validation across 7 in-domain and 3 out-of-domain datasets with 8 baseline methods, showing consistent improvements in utility across all three scenarios
Elegant technical design with well-justified reward function (Eq. 7) including thorough theoretical analysis of how the preference factor α and reliability factor γ influence model behavior
Strong empirical evidence that intrinsic self-assessment outperforms external routers (Table 5: 80% vs 71% accuracy), demonstrating the core motivation is valid
Practical modularity demonstrated through plug-and-play capability without retraining (Table 4), with clear system-level routing distribution shifts and agent-level answer rate adaptability

Excellent analysis of why DiSRouter routes better: superior discrimination between easy/hard queries (Figure 6), strong self-awareness ability (Figure 7), and comprehensive agent-level scenario adaptability analysis
Important control experiment (Appendix J) rigorously showing training improves self-awareness without improving task capability (<1% ΔPerformance), validating the source of improvements
Good generalization to out-of-domain tasks and high reproducibility with detailed implementation details, public datasets, and comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Architectural exploration severely limited: despite claiming support for tree/mesh structures, only cascade architecture is evaluated; no experimental validation of claimed generality weakens the modularity claims
Evaluation restricted to single model family (Qwen2.5-Instruct); generalization to other model families (GPT, Llama, Claude) and heterogeneous model pools entirely unexplored
Lacks theoretical analysis of optimality and convergence; distributed decomposition (Eq. 6) assumes agent independence but interactions may matter; 20-35% gap from oracle unexplained
Training design choices not deeply justified: rejection threshold δ = 1-α appears ad-hoc, equal balance of accepted/rejected samples unvalidated, γ = 0.5 chosen without ablation studies

Insufficient comparison with most related work (Automix); differences in implementation details not thoroughly analyzed, and sufficiency of single rejection decision vs. multiple verification steps unclear
No statistical significance testing, error bars, or confidence intervals; single-run results without robustness validation or multiple seeds
Cost model uses normalized abstract costs rather than real API pricing; routing cost accounting incomplete (rejection time only, not token generation during cascade)
Limited ablation studies: no isolated SFT vs. RL comparison, no sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters (γ, δ), only zero-shot CoT evaluation without other prompting strategies
Scalability claims underspecified: only tests 5→3 agent removal; no analysis of cascade efficiency with growing agent counts or retraining cost comparison vs. centralized approaches
Prompt engineering dependency for scenario adaptability not robustness-tested; robustness to prompt variation unexplored despite being critical for practical deployment

strengths: Well-motivated architectural contribution addressing real deployment limitations of centralized routers (inflexibility and inaccurate capability assessment)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 10 datasets, 8+ baselines, multiple scenarios, demonstrating consistent improvements (73% utility vs. 61% best baseline in Balance scenario)
Genuine modularity benefit demonstrated: 3-agent system maintains superior performance without retraining (Table 4), validating practical plug-and-play capability

Strong analytical insights showing intrinsic self-assessment (80% accuracy) substantially outperforms external routers (56-71%), with evidence that improvements come from routing decisions not task performance gains (Appendix A.8)

Generalization across multiple dimensions: different model families (Gemma-3, Phi-4), open-ended tasks (text summarization), and both open/closed-source LLMs, with detailed reproducibility information
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: self-awareness training closely follows Xu et al. (2024), SFT+RL is standard, main contribution is architectural rather than algorithmic

Cascade architecture highly restrictive: restricted evaluation to simple cascades; more flexible topologies (tree/mesh) acknowledged to require system-level information but not explored, limiting claims of general distributed routing

Lack of theoretical rigor: distributed optimization (Eq. 6) lacks formal justification that local utility maximization leads to global optimality; no convergence analysis or conditions for when local-global alignment holds

Incomplete experimental comparisons: main experiments use single model family (Qwen2.5); fairness with GraphRouter unclear (appears scenario-specific training vs. DiSRouter prompt adaptation); RouteLLM/Automix excluded from modularity test due to retraining requirements

Self-awareness training scalability concerns: requires N CoT trials per query during data construction; open-source models show poor intrinsic self-awareness (F1 scores 23-48), necessitating training whose cost vs. centralized routing is not analyzed

Routing overhead accumulation underestimated: while single rejection <5%, cascades to final model reach 4.46% overhead; multi-hop cascades compound overhead, potentially offsetting cost savings in optimization scenarios

Prompt-based scenario adaptability fragility: relies on prompt engineering (Table 22) for scenario control without robustness analysis; no study of sensitivity to prompt variations or guarantee of generalization across model families
Limited scalability validation: evaluated with only 5 agents (or 3 in modularity test); no experiments with 10+ agents to assess performance degradation with cascade depth or model pool size

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly articulates limitations of centralized routers (inflexibility, capability assessment bottlenecks)
Comprehensive experimental scope: 10 datasets, 8 baselines, 3 scenarios, generalization across domains and model families
Strong empirical results: achieves highest utility across all scenarios, reaching ~74% of Oracle topline performance
Practical advantages demonstrated: modularity without retraining, scenario adaptability via preference factor, reasonable average-case latency
Thorough post-hoc analysis: clear demonstration of better easy/hard query discrimination, intrinsic vs external assessment comparison, ablation on task capability improvement
Well-designed reward formulation: reliability factor γ is theoretically justified with clear intuition and formal analysis
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core idea (each LLM rejects uncertain queries instead of central router deciding) is relatively straightforward; heavily builds on rejection-based training from Xu et al. (2024) without substantial technical innovation

Methodological issues in baseline comparison: modified implementations (FrugalGPT/FORC substitute Qwen2.5-0.5B for DistilBERT), selective exclusions (RouteLLM/Automix from modularity tests), training asymmetry between DiSRouter and baselines

Confounded contributions: paper conflates (A) architectural benefits of distributed routing with (B) training benefits from self-awareness training; no clear ablation isolating these effects; comparison against trained centralized routers missing

Overstatement of generality: claims framework supports tree/mesh structures but only evaluates cascades; Discussion acknowledges needing additional 'system-level information' for other topologies; no experimental validation of claimed flexibility

Weak theoretical foundation: lacks principled explanation for why intrinsic assessment is fundamentally better than external routing; Table 5 shows external router performance scales with model size, suggesting this is resource tradeoff not architectural truth

Mixed out-of-domain generalization: OOD utility improvements modest (0.48 vs 0.39 for Balance, only 23% relative gain); DiSRouter SFT alone sometimes underperforms baselines; RL improvements incremental
Significant latency overhead in worst case: 0.241s vs 0.028s for GraphRouter (8.6× slower); contradicts claim of minimal overhead; cumulative rejection latency for cascades not properly addressed
Incomplete failure analysis: no characterization of query types causing misrouting; no explanation for occasional underperformance (e.g., cost-first scenario); missing error mode analysis

Scenario adaptability via prompting not architecturally novel: achieved through scenario-specific prompts (Table 22), not architectural changes; centralized routers could use identical prompting strategy
Limited ablation studies: no sensitivity to rejection threshold δ=1-α; no analysis of task-dependency; no study of training data scaling; only 10k samples with 1 epoch—potential underfitting
No statistical significance testing: despite 'extensive experiments,' no confidence intervals or hypothesis tests provided; improvements claimed without statistical rigor

Experimental setup limitations: primary results on single model family (Qwen2.5); cross-family validation shows mixed results; simple linear utility metric without justification or comparison to alternatives

strengths: Novel and well-motivated paradigm shift from centralized to distributed routing with clear identification of concrete limitations (inflexibility, limited capability assessment)

Strong technical contributions: localized reward function enables independent parallel training; elegant reward design (1-α)^γ captures nonlinear performance-cost preferences; scenario adaptability without retraining

Comprehensive and convincing experimental evaluation: 7 in-domain + 3 out-of-domain datasets, strong baselines, consistent improvements across all three preference scenarios (achieving ~74% of oracle utility)

Excellent analysis demonstrating superiority of intrinsic self-assessment: DiSRouter (80% F1) outperforms external classifiers (56-71% F1); discriminates query difficulty better than baselines (Figure 6); clear separation between answered and rejected query accuracy (Figure 7)

Modularity and flexibility well-demonstrated: 3-agent system works without retraining; generalizes across model families (Gemma, Phi); works with open-source and closed-source LLMs; scenario adaptability via single unified system

Strong reproducibility and transparency: detailed hyperparameters, comprehensive prompts, public datasets/models, ablation showing task performance unchanged (0.8% improvement), clear explanation of routing overhead (~4%)
Good generalization evidence: out-of-domain tasks, open-ended generative tasks, heterogeneous model pools; robust across diverse architectures and preference settings
Well-written with clear motivation, good use of figures and tables, thorough appendices with detailed experimental protocols
weaknesses: Limited architectural scope despite claims of generality: all experiments use cascade exclusively; claims about tree/mesh structures remain theoretical with no implementation, concrete design, or empirical validation despite positioning as 'general distributed routing framework'

Baseline implementation inconsistency raises fair comparison concerns: FrugalGPT and FORC use modified implementations (Qwen-0.5B instead of DistilBERT), justified only as 'poor performance in initial trials'; unclear if competing methods received equal hyperparameter search effort as GraphRouter's 'extensive' search

Incomplete analysis of intrinsic vs. external assessment: Table 5 compares DiSRouter (7B) against 8B LLM-based classifier (71% F1); missing ablation training 7B external classifier with identical SFT+RL data; current comparison confounds architecture with training, weakening intrinsic assessment claims

OOD performance degradation with RL training unexplained: Table 3 shows DiSRouter SFT (0.74) outperforms DiSRouter+RL (0.69) in balance scenario on OOD data; suggests overfitting to in-domain distributions without explanation or mitigation strategy

Scenario adaptability achieved primarily through prompt engineering with α parameter—somewhat incremental and not novel beyond existing instruction-tuning work; missing ablation comparing single prompt across α values vs. scenario-specific prompts

Limited scale: maximum pool size 5 models; real deployments may use 10-20+ models; no analysis of computational scaling with pool size; action space constraint (only route to higher-cost models) restrictive and unjustified

Training data construction mismatches evaluation: uses greedy decoding for correctness labels but tests with temperature=1 sampling; threshold δ=1-α appears heuristic without rigorous justification; no comparison of alternative labeling strategies

Theoretical gaps: no formal analysis of whether distributed local optimization (Eq. 6) converges to system optimum (Eq. 5); missing approximation ratio analysis vs. oracle; γ=0.5 choice based on curve inspection rather than principled design or sensitivity analysis
